meta.title: Who really said "Everyone has been made for some particular work, and the desire for that work has been put in every heart"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Rumi did write it — Masnavi Book III, line 1618. But Nicholson’s 1930 translation reads “put into his heart,” not “in every heart.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Everyone has been made for some particular work, and the desire for that work has been put in every heart'?
meta.ogDescription: The couplet is real Rumi: Masnavi III.1618. The popular English ending “in every heart” is a loosened version of Nicholson’s 1930 translation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Rumi’s: the couplet sits in the Masnavi, Book III, line 1618, and R. A. Nicholson’s 1930 translation renders it “Every one has been made for some particular work, and the desire for that (work) has been put into his heart.” Nicholson’s “his” is distributive — it points back to the “Every one” that opens the same line — so the popular ending “in every heart” does not change the sense. What it lacks is a source: no published translation has been shown to carry that wording, and Wikiquote files it under Attributed with a 1997 book about creativity as its only citation.

source.excerpt:
Every one has been made for some particular work, and the desire for that (work) has been put into his heart.
How should hand and foot be set in motion without desire? How should sticks and straws go (from their place) without any water or wind?
trail: The Persian couplet and its English are set side by side at Masnavi Book 3, line 1618 ↗; the site states on its FAQ page that “The English is by RA Nicholson” ↗.

The printed volume confirms it. Volume IV of Nicholson’s Mathnawi ↗ — title page: “Containing the Translation of the Third & Fourth Books,” printed by Cambridge University Press for the Trustees of the “E. J. W. Gibb Memorial” and published by Luzac & Co., London, 1930 — carries the line between the printed verse markers 1615 and 1620, and reads “put into his heart.”

The popular wording is not treated as sourced. Wikiquote places it in its Attributed section ↗, citing Jan Phillips, Marry Your Muse: Making a Lasting Commitment to Your Creativity (1997) p. 75 — not an edition of Rumi. Quote Investigator has no article on this line.
In general circulation it carries no source at all: BrainyQuote lists the ‘every heart’ form under Rumi with no work or translator named ↗.
source.excerptNote: Nicholson’s translation, Masnavi Book III, lines 1618–1619. His “his heart” is distributive: grammatically singular, but bound to the “Every one” that opens the same line, exactly as the Persian is (har kasī … dilash). The verses leading up to it are general too — 1616, “Just as staying at home is easy to us, so travelling is easy to another class of people.” So “in every heart” is a loose rendering, not a change of scope; it is simply not the wording of any identified published translation. The Persian couplet reads “هر کسی را بهر کاری ساختند / میل آن را در دلش انداختند.”

source.useLine: Two different strings, two different answers. Nicholson’s 1930 English — “Every one has been made for some particular work, and the desire for that (work) has been put into his heart” — is in the public domain in the United States and free to use, including commercially; so is the thirteenth-century Persian beneath it. The popular “in every heart” ending is a different matter: no publication or translator has been identified for it, so this page claims no rights status for that wording. For a slide, use Nicholson’s line, credited as shown above.
source.rightsNote: Rumi composed the Masnavi in Persian in the thirteenth century, so the original is long out of copyright. The English shown above is Reynold A. Nicholson’s, first published in Volume IV of his Mathnawi (Luzac & Co., London, 1930) ↗ — before 1931, and therefore in the public domain in the United States. No rights status is claimed for the loosened “in every heart” wording that circulates online, because no publication or translator for it has been identified.

author.name: Rumi
author.heading: Who was Rumi?
author.metaLine: 1207–1273 · Persian poet, Islamic scholar and Sufi mystic
author.bio: Jalāl al-Dīn Muḥammad Rūmī was born on 30 September 1207 in Wakhsh, in what is now Tajikistan, and died on 17 December 1273 in Konya, in present-day Turkey. A jurist and preacher before he was a poet, his encounter with the wandering mystic Shams of Tabriz turned him into one of the most prolific spiritual writers in any language; the order founded in his name became known in the West for its whirling dervishes. His masterwork, the Masnavi — six books and roughly 25,000 verses, dictated from about 1258 until his death — has been called “a Qur’an in Persian,” and he is today among the most widely read poets in the United States.

misattribution.heading: What actually went wrong
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake Rumi quote — and that makes it unusual. The couplet is real and locatable. What drifted is the last six words, and then the citation trail vanished behind them.

items.why: Nicholson’s translation reads “Every one has been made for some particular work, and the desire for that (work) has been put into his heart” — where “his” is distributive, bound to the “Every one” in the same line. The drift is therefore in the words, not the meaning: “in every heart” says what Nicholson says, but it is not what he wrote, and no other published translation has been found that does. The 1930 volume is scanned in full at the Internet Archive ↗.

This is the only source Wikiquote offers for the wording ↗, and it files the line under Attributed rather than among the sourced Masnavi passages. A book about creative practice is where the phrasing is documented; it is not where Rumi wrote.

The line travels with a name and nothing else. BrainyQuote prints it under Rumi with no work, edition or translator ↗, which is why almost nobody encountering it can tell that a genuine couplet sits underneath.

misattribution.truthLine: Rumi wrote it. He wrote it in Persian, in the Masnavi, at Book III, line 1618 ↗ — and the English you have seen is a softened echo of the one careful translation that carried it over.

context.heading: Why the line matters
lead: The couplet does not appear in a vacuum. In Nicholson’s translation it falls inside the “Story of the dervish who had secluded himself in the mountains” ↗, where Rumi is defending temperament against prescription: staying home is easy for one person and travelling easy for another; one man loves dominion, another loves the ironsmith’s handicraft. The line about particular work is the conclusion he draws from that ordinary observation.

What follows it is the part the internet drops. The very next verse asks, “How should hand and foot be set in motion without desire? How should sticks and straws go (from their place) without any water or wind?” Rumi is not promising that your calling will feel good — he is arguing that desire is the mechanism by which anything moves at all, and then warning you to check which way yours points before you follow it.
context.detailsSummary: Why Rumi in English drifts so far from Rumi in Persian
detailsBody: Reynold A. Nicholson’s eight-volume edition, described by the Encyclopaedia of Islam as “the classic edition” ↗, gave English readers the first complete translation of the Masnavi. It is scrupulous to the point of awkwardness — the parenthetical “(work)” in this very line marks a word Nicholson supplied for sense rather than found in the Persian.

Almost everything else in English is looser. The scholarly site Dar al-Masnavi devotes a long page to correcting popular renderings, noting that such “creative versions” rarely sound like Rumi to anyone reading the original, and are often shockingly altered ↗. The shift here is milder than most — Nicholson’s distributive “his heart” and the popular “every heart” carry the same sense — but it is the same mechanism: a scrupulous rendering replaced by a smoother one, which then travels with no translator’s name attached to it.
